summary_html: CPS **accepts** a report for **investigation/assessment**. CAPTA sets the floor for investigation procedures; CFSR evaluates timeliness, safety, and decision quality.
authority_html:

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit held that social workers are bound by the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement when entering a home and that no social-worker exception exists, but granted qualified immunity because that rule was not clearly established in the circuit at the time of the entry.
key_cases.relevance: Once a report is accepted for investigation, entry into the home requires consent, exigency or a warrant, and the agency bears the burden on consent.
key_cases.quote: we agree that a social worker, like other state officers, is governed by the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Amendment governs a social worker's in-school interview of a child during a child-abuse investigation, requiring at a minimum reasonable suspicion of abuse, and the court affirmed denial of qualified immunity on the children's Fourth Amendment claims and on the parents' Fourteenth Amendment claims arising from a coercive in-home safety plan.
key_cases.relevance: It sets the minimum evidentiary predicate for the investigative interview of a child once a report is accepted.
key_cases.quote: a social worker must have a reasonable suspicion of child abuse before conducting an in-school interview when no other exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement applies

key_cases.holding: A child victim's statements made for purposes of medical diagnosis or treatment are admissible under Evid.R. 803(4) regardless of whether the child has been found competent to testify, and their admission did not violate the Confrontation Clause.
key_cases.relevance: How an investigative interview is framed — treatment-directed or forensic — determines whether the child's statements are later admissible.
key_cases.quote: the child's statements may be admitted at trial as an exception to the hearsay rule pursuant to Evid.R. 803(4) if they were made for purposes of medical diagnosis or treatment

key_cases.holding: In a suit over a child's death, the Court held that a public children services agency and its employees owe no R.C. 2151.421(A)(1)(a) duty to cross-report an incoming referral to law enforcement, that R.C. 2919.22 does not expressly impose liability on them, and that employee immunity is lost only for recklessness, which requires a perverse disregard of a known risk rather than mere negligence.
key_cases.relevance: The opinion sets the liability floor for how an accepted referral is investigated by agency staff.
key_cases.quote: a public children services agency and its employees, upon receipt of a case referral, do not have a duty under R.C. 2151.421(A)(1)(a) to cross-report the case to a law-enforcement agency

key_cases.case_name: Gersper v. Ashtabula County Children Services Board
key_cases.holding: Former R.C. 2151.421(G) immunized a children services board and its caseworker from a negligent-investigation suit because, although as recipients of the report they were not 'participating in the making of reports,' they did participate in the judicial proceeding that resulted from the report; the Court distinguished Brodie, where the agency received reports of abuse and failed to act at all.
key_cases.relevance: An agency that investigates and goes to court on a report is immune, while Brodie denies immunity to an agency that receives reports and does nothing — the line that governs the accept-for-investigation decision.
key_cases.quote: former R.C. 2151.421(G) confers immunity upon those who, as a result of a report of a known or suspected incident of child abuse and/or neglect, participate in a judicial proceeding

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Sitting en banc in an Ohio case, the court reversed summary judgment based on absolute immunity, holding that a caseworker is absolutely immune only for acts performed as a legal advocate and not for out-of-court administrative or investigative conduct, so a caseworker who allegedly concealed from the juvenile court that the mother had been located, and concealed the pendency of the permanent-custody decision from her, was not absolutely immune.
key_cases.relevance: Holloway is the source of the functional test that leaves investigative and administrative caseworker conduct exposed to suit, which is what makes investigation-stage misconduct actionable at all.
key_cases.quote: social workers are absolutely immune only when they are acting in their capacity as legal advocates - initiating court actions or testifying under oath

timeline_requirements.deadline: If face-to-face safety contacts are completed within 4 working days: safety assessment recorded in Ohio's CCWIS within 10 working days and approved within 2 working days of submission (OAC 5180:3-5-01(D)(2)). If they are not completed within 4 working days: attempts continue and the safety assessment is recorded and approved within 3 working days after the face-to-face contacts are completed (OAC 5180:3-5-01(D)(3))
No later than 60 days (family assessment recorded and approved)
